records.title: Every MCP tool call blocks ~54s on telemetry unless DATAHUB_TELEMETRY_ENABLED=false
records.body:
## What happens

Every MCP tool call blocks for ~54 seconds unless `DATAHUB_TELEMETRY_ENABLED=false` is set. The stall is per call, not per session, so anything that issues many tool calls becomes unusable.

Found while running a lineage traversal that issues thousands of `get_lineage_paths_between` calls: it timed out after 50 minutes. With telemetry disabled the same traversal finishes in **70 seconds**.

## Measurement

Same GMS, same data, same machine, minutes apart. Only the environment variable changed.

| Call | default | `DATAHUB_TELEMETRY_ENABLED=false` |
|---|---|---|
| `list_schema_fields` (returns 8 fields) | 54.32s | **0.09s** |
| `get_lineage` (returns 4 datasets) | 53.77s | — |
| `get_lineage_paths_between` | 53.84s / 53.78s / 53.91s | — |

Repeated calls with telemetry disabled: 0.30s, 0.09s, 0.09s.

## Why this is not query cost

Three independent reasons:

1. **`list_schema_fields` returning 8 fields cannot take 54 seconds.** There is no work there to be slow.
2. **The duration is near-constant across three different tools** — 53.77 to 54.32 — which is the signature of a fixed timeout, not of query work that would vary with result size.
3. **The same question answered through GraphQL takes 0.39s.** Asking for the upstream lineage of one column via `searchAcrossLineage` against the same GMS:

   ```
   graphql ping             0.31s
   searchAcrossLineage col  0.39s   -> total=4
   MCP get_lineage         53.77s   -> 4 datasets
   MCP list_schema_fields  54.32s   -> 8 fields
   ```

So the backend is answering promptly and the MCP layer is adding a fixed ~54s on top.

## Environment

- `mcp-server-datahub` launched via `uvx mcp-server-datahub@latest`
- `acryl-datahub` 1.6.0.15, DataHub Core GMS v1.5.0.6 (quickstart)
- Windows 11, Python 3.11

## The caveat, stated rather than hidden

I have not isolated which endpoint the telemetry path contacts, and I can only report what this environment does. If telemetry reaches a remote endpoint and this network path is slow to it, the 54s may not reproduce elsewhere — the magnitude is environment-dependent by nature.

But the shape seems worth reporting regardless of the exact number: **a tool call that blocks on telemetry is a tool call that inherits the telemetry path's latency**, and a timeout there costs a caller their whole session rather than degrading. Failing fast, backgrounding the send, or capping it with a short timeout would each remove the coupling.

Confirmation from someone on a different network would be useful, and I am happy to gather more detail — a packet capture or a profile of the blocking call — if that would help narrow it.

records.title: [Enhancement]: RFC: Support nested collections / collection hierarchies
records.body:
### Type of Enhancement

Server Backend

### Describe the Feature/Enhancement

**Summary**
I would like to propose support for organizing collections into a parent/child hierarchy.

Collections are currently flat: a collection belongs to a library and contains books, but it cannot contain or reference child collections. This works well for small libraries, but becomes difficult to navigate when a library contains large franchises, fictional universes, publishers, subjects, or other groups that naturally have subdivisions.

This RFC proposes a deliberately small, backwards-compatible implementation based on an optional self-referencing parentId. Before working on a PR, I would like maintainer feedback on whether this feature fits Audiobookshelf and whether a server-and-web-first contribution would be acceptable.

**Example use case**
Imagine a sizeable Dungeons & Dragons ebook library. Ideally, it would be presented as:
```
Dungeons & Dragons
├─+ [Adventures]                 (5 books)
├─+ [Expansions]                 (4 books)
├─  Dungeon Master's Guide
├─  Monster Manual 
└─  Player's Handbook
```
Today, the closest approximation is three unrelated, prefixed collections:
```
Dungeons & Dragons — Core
Dungeons & Dragons — Expansions
Dungeons & Dragons — Adventures
```
The prefix keeps them adjacent when sorting by name, but it does not preserve the relationship between them. There is no single Dungeons & Dragons entry point, breadcrumb, collapsible tree, or way to browse from the parent context into one of the categories.

The same problem occurs with other large universes and organizational schemes, for example:
```
Star Wars
├── Canon
│   ├── High Republic
│   └── New Republic
└── Legends

History
├── Ancient
├── Medieval
└── Modern
```
**Proposed user-facing behavior**
A collection can optionally have one parent collection. Collections without a parent remain root collections.

A minimal web UI would:

1. Show only root collections on the main Collections shelf.
2. Show child collections near the top of a parent collection page.
3. Show a breadcrumb when browsing a child, for example Dungeons & Dragons / Adventures.
4. Add an optional Parent collection selector to the create/edit collection dialog.
5. Continue showing directly assigned books below any child collections.
6. For an MVP, drag-and-drop tree editing would not be required. Selecting a parent in the existing edit dialog would be sufficient.

**Proposed data and API design**
The proposed model adds an optional self-reference to a collection:
```json
{
  "id": "collection-id",
  "libraryId": "library-id",
  "name": "Child collection name",
  "parentId": "parent-collection-id",
  "books": ["library-item-id"]
}
```
Root collections would use parentId: null.

Validation rules:

- A collection may have at most one parent, producing a tree rather than a graph.
- Parent and child must belong to the same library.
- A collection cannot be its own parent.
- Assignments that would create a cycle must be rejected.
- Existing permission and content restrictions must still apply when listing or opening descendants.
- Because each collection points to at most one parent, the same model supports arbitrary nesting depth without requiring a separate design for each level.

For backward compatibility, the existing endpoints would continue returning a flat collection list with an additional nullable parentId. Existing clients can ignore the new field, while hierarchy-aware clients can build the tree from the flat response. No separate tree endpoint or other breaking API change is proposed.

**Parent contents and aggregation**
Parent collections would continue to contain directly assigned books and can additionally have child collections. Descendant books would not be duplicated or aggregated into the parent's books array.

Actions such as Play all, Create playlist, and RSS feeds would continue to operate only on books directly assigned to the current collection. Recursive aggregation is outside the scope of this change because it would introduce new ordering and duplicate-handling semantics.

**Deletion and move semantics**
Deleting a parent would not delete its child collections. Before deleting the parent, its direct children would be moved to the root level by setting their parentId to null. Cascading deletion is not proposed.

Moving a collection would update only its parent relationship. It would not move or duplicate any books.

**Backward compatibility and migration**
A migration would initialize all existing collections with parentId = null, preserving the current flat structure.

Existing behavior should remain unchanged when no hierarchy is configured:

- existing collection URLs and IDs remain valid;
- existing book membership and ordering remain unchanged;
- existing API clients can continue treating collections as a flat list;
- existing socket events can add the optional field without changing their event names;
- libraries that do not use nesting should look and behave as they do today.

**Scope proposed for a first PR**

In scope:

- nullable parent relationship in the server model;
- migration for existing collections;
- same-library and cycle validation;
- arbitrary hierarchy depth;
- create/update API support;
- additive API serialization;
- parent selector, child cards, and breadcrumbs in the web client;
- tests for migration, validation, serialization, and deletion behavior.

Potential follow-ups, rather than MVP requirements:

- arbitrary drag-and-drop ordering of sibling collections;
- recursive Play all, playlist creation, or RSS feeds;
- empty organizational collections;
- smart/dynamic child collections;
- multiple parents;
- cross-library hierarchies;
- automatic hierarchy generation from folders, tags, or series;
- mobile-client-specific navigation changes.

**Related requests**
This proposal is related to, but distinct from:

#870 — nested series / adding a whole series to a collection;
#4996 — deeper series hierarchi

records.title: [Enhancement]: RFC: Introduce paginated relational Collection API alongside legacy endpoints
records.body:
### Type of Enhancement

Server Backend

### Describe the Feature/Enhancement

This proposal is in response to the direction described by `advplyr` in the nested-collections RFC #5452: "the current Collection API preserves the old response shape on top of the relational model, and a new API should be introduced alongside it before adding more Collection complexity."

Therefor I propose introducing a new paginated Collection read API alongside the existing legacy endpoints. The goal is to provide a stable relational API that clients can adopt incrementally without breaking existing integrations.

The new API should:

- return lightweight collection summaries instead of every book in every collection;
- paginate both collection lists and individual collection contents at the database level;
- support collection sorting and optional name filtering;
- apply library, tag, and explicit-content permissions before pagination and serialization;
- leave the existing Collection endpoints unchanged during client migration;
- provide a response model that can later accommodate nested collections and mixed book/collection ordering.

### Goals

1. Add a new, non-breaking Collection read API based on the relational data model.
2. Paginate before loading expanded library-item data.
3. Return compact summaries from collection-list endpoints.
4. Preserve existing permission semantics without leaking inaccessible counts or preview items.
5. Support sorting by collection name, with room for additional sort fields.
6. Allow the server web client and other clients to migrate incrementally.
7. Keep the API shape extensible for nested collections without implementing nesting in this RFC.

### Non-goals

This proposal does not include:

- removing or changing existing Collection endpoints;
- implementing nested collections or a `parentId` migration;
- recursive collection contents;
- empty organizational collections;
- changing Collection create, update, delete, RSS, playlist, or Play All behavior;
- replacing the existing manual book order;
- mixed book/child-collection ordering in the initial implementation;
- immediate deprecation of legacy endpoints.

### Maintainer feedback requested

I would be happy to contribute this in focused, reviewable steps. The design is intended as a concrete default rather than a list of open-ended alternatives.

The one blocking architectural question before implementation is:

> Is an explicit `/api/v2` namespace acceptable for these new Collection contracts, or should they use a different versioning or path convention?

### Related issues and pull requests

- #5452 - RFC: Support nested collections / collection hierarchies.
- #3569 - Add to Collection is slow or crashes, especially on mobile.
- #5170 - Collections page loads a 54 MB response with `minified=1`.
- #4836 - Get All Collections API is very slow; closed as a duplicate of #3569.
- #1836 - Sorting options for Collections.
- #5358 - Applies minified serialization inside legacy Collection responses; useful mitigation, but not database pagination.

### Why would this be helpful?

The current Collection endpoints can return very large responses and consume substantial server and client resources. Users have reported slow or crashing collection dialogs, a 54 MB Collections response despite requesting `minified=1`, and very slow Get All Collections calls.[2][3][4]

The underlying problem is structural rather than only a serialization issue:

1. `GET /api/collections` loads every collection through the legacy expanded serializer.[7][9]
2. `GET /api/libraries/{libraryId}/collections` accepts `page` and `limit`, but currently loads and serializes all matching collections before slicing the result in memory.[8]
3. The legacy model query eager-loads every collection's books, library items, authors, and series to reproduce the pre-relational response shape.[7]
4. Permission filtering happens after those records have already been materialized.[7]
5. A collection list or selection dialog usually needs only collection metadata, an accessible item count, and at most a small cover preview.

Applying minified serialization, as proposed in PR #5358, is a useful short-term reduction in payload size, but it does not add database pagination or prevent all collection memberships from being loaded.[6]

A relational, database-paginated API would make response size and server work proportional to the requested page size instead of the total number of collections and memberships. This should improve:

- Collections page load time;
- performance on "Add to Collection" dialogs, especially on mobile;
- server memory use and database load;
- client memory use and rendering time;
- scalability for users with large libraries or many collections;
- the feasibility of future features such as nested collections. ;-)

It would also create a clear migration path: legacy clients can continue using the current contract while first-party and third-party clients adopt the new endpoints independently.

### Future Implementation (Screenshot)

### 1. List collection summaries for a library

```http
GET /api/v2/libraries/{libraryId}/collections
    ?page=0
    &limit=20
    &sort=name
    &desc=0
    &filter=dungeons
```

Proposed query parameters:

| Parameter | Default | Description |
|---|---:|---|
| `page` | `0` | Zero-based page number |
| `limit` | `20` | Number of results, bounded by a server maximum such as 100 |
| `sort` | `name` | Initially `name`, `createdAt`, or `updatedAt` |
| `desc` | `0` | Descending sort when set to `1` |
| `filter` | empty | Optional case-insensitive name filter |

Proposed response:

```json
{
  "results": [
    {
      "id": "collection-id",
      "libraryId": "library-id",
      "name": "Dungeons & Dragons",
      "description": null,
      "numBooks": 42,
      "previewItems": [
        {
          "id": "library-item-id",
          "media": {
            "coverPath": "/metadata/items/.../cover.jpg"
          }
        }

records.title: Workplane M2E: fixed work-item lifecycle and dependency DAG
records.body:
## Purpose

Complete the next smallest graph-safe Track B portion of the frozen M2 durable core: public work items with the fixed lifecycle and a typed cross-project dependency graph over the accepted M2D ledger/outbox/replay/realtime substrate.

Exact implementation base: `4f766f940a42a52e945dfc4753e9f847d28c06b9`.

This is the sole release-bearing product unit. WIP remains `1`; recursive depth remains `0`.

## Acceptance criteria

1. **Public work-item contract.** OpenAPI, generated Go/TypeScript consumers, examples, permission mapping, and the production server expose create/list/get/update, assign, transition, and atomic project batch-transition operations. Required request members are presence-aware at the raw HTTP boundary, and every operation is available to humans and equivalently scoped agents through the same public plane.
2. **Fixed lifecycle and derived blocking.** The server enforces only `open -> in_progress -> in_review -> done`, `in_review -> in_progress`, and cancellation from each nonterminal state, with optimistic versions and target-bound idempotency. `blocked` is derived from unresolved blocking dependencies or hard gates and is never persisted as a work-item state. Reaching `done` never substitutes for deliverable acceptance.
3. **Typed dependency graph.** Dependencies are exactly `blocks`, `relates`, or `caused-by`; endpoints belong to one organization, may cross projects within that organization, and preserve private-project non-disclosure. Only `blocks` participates in cycle detection. Self-cycles and direct or transitive blocking cycles return the typed `dependency_cycle` error before commit, while `relates` and `caused-by` cannot create false cycle failures.
4. **Atomic concurrency semantics.** Work-item transitions, assignment, dependency add/remove, and multi-item batch transitions require current authorization and expected versions. A batch either commits every requested item/event/outbox/idempotency record or leaves zero residue. Concurrent inverse-edge creation cannot commit a blocking cycle; stale versions, duplicate targets, missing items, mixed organizations, and permission failures also leave zero partial state.
5. **Authorization and parity.** Every read/write checks actor, organization, concrete project/resource, current project role, delegated human/agent intersection, token action scope, project restriction, expiry, and revocation before returning stored idempotent results or writing. Human and equivalently scoped agent responses, errors, side effects, events, and realtime envelopes match field-for-field; invalid or denied attempts do not update agent token last-used state.
6. **Durable integration.** Every accepted command atomically updates relational state, versioned domain events, canonical outbox, replay/checksum projections, integrity doctor inputs, and WebSocket/SSE delivery. Replay reproduces lifecycle, assignment, dependency edges, and derived blocking deterministically. Unknown/tampered events, post-row database errors, projection drift, and corrupt dependency state fail closed without advancing a known-good projection head.
7. **Upgrade and load-bearing evidence.** A real-PostgreSQL M2D-to-M2E migration preserves every accepted row/event/outbox/checkpoint and backfills or rejects any required new state atomically. Named real-stack tests cover lifecycle edges, bounce, cancellation, assignment, cross-project dependencies, direct/transitive and concurrent cycle rejection, dependency removal/unblocking, atomic batch success/failure, parity, authorization/no-leak behavior, replay, restart, realtime, and fault boundaries. Removing the production lifecycle, DAG, authorization, batch-atomicity, replay, or fail-closed guards must make the corresponding named gate fail for its intended semantic reason.
8. **Exact-source evidence and scope.** The existing full Workplane smoke/evidence suite remains green and a clean exact-head manifest records commands, timestamps, counts, PostgreSQL outcomes, replay/checksums, realtime results, mutation proofs, and artifact digests. No project terminal commands, exploration hypotheses/experiments, inbox/judgment projection, comments, search, structured briefs, Track C UI, CRDT/Yjs, ECA, generalized automation, release/scale claim, second product lane, or frozen-repository access is introduced.

## Required PR trailers

`Closes #<this issue>`

`Advances #1`

records.title: M0: Stabilize orderbook-rs before trader-rs depends on it
records.body:
## Objective

Fix the two known correctness bugs in this library and add regression coverage, before `trader-rs` starts depending on it.

`trader-rs` is building a live Binance market-data feed handler and will use this crate to hold the local order book. The single value its first milestone publishes is top of book, so `get_best_price` is that milestone's entire output. We are not building on a dependency with known defects in exactly that path.

## Scope

Correctness only.

Explicitly **not** in this milestone:

* order-book redesign;
* L2 / price-level API such as `set_level()`;
* data-structure or performance optimisation;
* changes to unrelated APIs.

The L2 versus L3 API question is real and is deferred to `trader-rs` M2, after the simple partial-snapshot slice is working.

## Checklist

* [ ] #22 Fix best bid / best ask semantics
* [ ] #20 Fix reinsertion of previously emptied price levels

Recommended order: #22 first. It is the only one that blocks `trader-rs` M1, it is the smaller change, and both fixes live in `book_side.rs` on non-overlapping lines.

Tracked separately, outside this milestone: #21 (stop tracking build artefacts).

## Downstream

`trader-rs` M1 is blocked on this milestone. That repository is private, so its issues will not be visible from here to anyone else.

records.title: PRD: sandcastle-synth two-loop AFK workflow wrapper
records.body:
## Problem Statement

Users want to run approved implementation slices hands-off while still preserving a strong human-approved contract. Plain Sandcastle already provides excellent agent execution, sandboxing, worktrees, branch strategies, prompt templates, completion signals, structured output, logs, commits, and merge-agent patterns, but it does not own the Alejo-specific contract pipeline: approved PRD/SAD/issues, Alejo Dev Plan approval, automatic BDD behavior scenarios, an inner TDD loop, synthetic-user validation through real interfaces, recommendation-driven repair, run reports, and deterministic GitHub issue updates.

Without `sandcastle-synth`, teams have to choose between fast AFK coding and confidence that the right user behavior was built. A normal agent implementation loop can pass local tests while missing the intended behavior. A normal acceptance test can describe the right behavior but fail to feed a useful next red test back into the coding loop. The missing product is a workflow wrapper that lets BDD define the contract, TDD build the code, and synthetic users validate the contract through real interfaces.

## Solution

Build `sandcastle-synth` as a workflow wrapper over the upstream Sandcastle API. The first public surface is the Synth CLI command `sandcastle-synth auto --plan <plan-file>`, which consumes the human-approved Alejo Dev Plan and runs the autonomous two-loop build.

The wrapper will parse the approved plan, preflight the run, schedule ready slices by dependency and `maxConcurrency`, create one Sandcastle-managed slice worktree per issue, generate a Given/When/Then `BehaviorScenario`, run the inner TDD loop in hard-isolated agent roles, run a separate synthetic tester agent through the selected verification surface, convert behavioral gaps into `recommendation.json`, feed those recommendations back into sequential TDD mini-cycles, and then merge completed slice branches through a dedicated merge phase.

The implementation should extend Sandcastle at the workflow layer, not reimplement Sandcastle primitives. Sandcastle remains responsible for sandboxes, worktrees, branch strategies, agent execution, logs, commit collection, prompt handling, provider factories, and merge-agent execution patterns. `sandcastle-synth` owns the Alejo contract, scheduler, BDD/TDD orchestration, synthetic-user verdicts, reports, and issue updates.

## User Stories

1. As a product owner, I want an approved Alejo Dev Plan to be the only launchable input, so that AFK execution cannot begin from a draft contract.
2. As a maintainer, I want `sandcastle-synth auto --plan <plan-file>` to fail fast on invalid plans, so that bad scheduler input does not waste agent budget.
3. As a maintainer, I want the scheduler block to be authoritative over the human-readable table, so that automation reads one exact contract.
4. As a maintainer, I want the command to reject unapproved plans, so that a written plan is not mistaken for human approval.
5. As a maintainer, I want every slice to map to an open `ready-for-agent` GitHub issue, so that only approved implementation slices enter the AFK pipeline.
6. As a maintainer, I want missing required secrets to stop the entire launch, so that no slice begins in an environment that cannot satisfy the plan.
7. As a maintainer, I want unsupported agent providers to be rejected before scheduling, so that the run cannot fail later because a provider was only vocabulary.
8. As a maintainer, I want the wrapper to use upstream Sandcastle worktrees and branch strategies, so that slice isolation follows the foundation project.
9. As a maintainer, I want each slice to run on a branch named from its issue number, so that branches are inspectable and traceable.
10. As a maintainer, I want `maxConcurrency` to limit active slices, so that AFK execution is parallel but bounded.
11. As a maintainer, I want dependencies between issues to control scheduling order, so that downstream slices do not start before their prerequisites are complete.
12. As a developer, I want one automatically generated `BehaviorScenario` per slice, so that the BDD contract is derived from approved artifacts rather than handwritten during execution.
13. As a developer, I want behavior scenarios to use Given/When/Then, so that the contract is readable and behavior-oriented.
14. As a developer, I want scenarios to use one happy-path assertion, two boundary assertions, and two quality-attribute assertions where justified, so that coverage is broad without becoming unbounded.
15. As a developer, I want missing assertion slots to carry skip reasons, so that the system does not invent checks unsupported by the source artifacts.
16. As a developer, I want missing acceptance criteria to produce a diagnostic scenario, so that the pipeline reports the contract problem clearly.
17. As a developer, I want contradictions between issue, PRD, and SAD context to fail closed, so that the synthetic user does not validate against a confused contract.
18. As a developer, I want the inner TDD loop to use hard context isolation, so that test writing, implementation, and refactoring are separate agent invocations.
19. As a developer, I want the TDD loop to be based on the referenced TDD workflow foundation, so that the red/green/refactor discipline is preserved without depending on Claude-only slash commands.
20. As a developer, I want each TDD mini-cycle to run the targeted red test and the configured full project verification command, so that local correctness is not narrowly faked.
21. As a developer, I want the synthetic user to run as a separate tester agent, so that BDD validation is independent from the coding agent.
22. As a developer, I want synthetic users to exercise `api`, `ui`, `cli`, or `mcp` surfaces, so that behavior is validated through real user-observable interfaces.
23. As a developer, I want every verification surface to have a typed adapter contract, so that behavior results are normalized across

records.title: TASK-C558-1: a .dig file parses as untrusted XML through a confinement-proven, StAX-bounded front door — XXE-proof, no reflective deserialization, test sections preserved
records.body:
## Abstract

Digital's `.dig` file — XStream's XML serialization of Digital's own object graph — cannot be opened by JLS today: no XML parser of any kind exists anywhere in `src/`, and the file must be read as hostile input, never as a trusted object-graph deserialization stream (XStream's default unmarshalling is a documented RCE primitive, the CVE-2021-39144 family). This task adds a StAX-based, bounded, XXE-hardened reader that parses `.dig` through `jls.imp.xml`, a shared XML front door #451 (TASK-0054) is building with this task as its designed second client, and registers `.dig` as the first contribution to the still-pending `Importer` extension point (`docs/extension-points.md`). The reader never reconstructs a Java object graph, is confined to one package by a bytecode-checked rule, and preserves Digital's embedded test sections character-recoverably for #562's downstream `-t` vector translation. Element mapping, generics, layout and the CLI invocation door are explicitly out of scope, owned respectively by #614, #615, #617 and #956.

## Intended Audience & Impact

- **Instructors authoring, grading, or auto-checking work in batch (`-b`) mode.** Today `jls -b course.dig` fails immediately at one of `JLSStart`'s hardcoded "is not a valid circuit file name" gates (§2 O9) with no path forward at all. This task is the first stage that lets such a file be *read* — safely, as hostile input — without exposing the instructor's machine to XXE, entity-expansion bombs, or XStream's reflective-deserialization RCE class. It does not by itself hand the instructor a working circuit; that requires #614 (mapping), #615 (generics), #617 (layout) and #956 (the CLI door) on top of this parse stage.
- **Students and circuit-file authors** with existing Digital coursework benefit once the full #558 pipeline lands; this task is a necessary but not sufficient stage toward that.
- **Contributors, maintainers, and LLM agents working the codebase.** The confinement rule and the extension-point registration this task adds are the pattern the two sibling parsers (#621 `.cv`, #629 Falstad) are expected to reuse, and they close one row of `docs/extension-points.md`'s "pending" table (§2 O8) rather than adding a fifth format-specific branch to `JLSStart` (§2 O9).

## Status & Dependencies

The evidence commit below predates any of this task's own code: `jls.imp.xml` does not exist in the tree at this commit (§2 O2), so every statement in this body about "consuming `jls.imp.xml`" is a statement about a contract #451 is building, not about code that exists today. Re-verify §2's observations at pickup, and re-derive citations if HEAD has moved (rule 6).

```yaml
tier: task
evidence_commit: c5cee1baff3451a85787b4a09bd0b2b05af7dfdd
part_of_feature: 558   # FEAT-C29-2 — the .dig converter pipeline this task is one stage of
blocked_by: [314]      # FEAT-002, literal translation of the pre-migration body's
                        # `ordering_after: [314]`. Two 2026-08-08 reviews asked that #451
                        # (part_of_feature 323) be added here too, since #451 is building the
                        # jls.imp.xml front door this task consumes; that request was never
                        # adopted and no reasoning for declining it was ever recorded. Left
                        # un-added here, pending maintainer disposition — see Open Questions.
blocks: [614, 617, 956] # 614 (TASK-C558-2) and 617 (TASK-C558-4) each carry this task in their
                        # own ordering_after; 956 (TASK-C558-6) carries ordering_after:[612]
                        # naming this task's AC-7 registry shape as the seam it routes through.
related: [38, 323, 451, 558, 562, 621, 629]
```

## 1. Background & Prior Work

`.circ` (Logisim-Evolution) opened the same "untrusted foreign format" problem this task solves for Digital. #451 (TASK-0054) is building `jls.imp.xml` explicitly as shared infrastructure: "A new shared package, `jls.imp.xml` — the hardened intake front door, designed for more than one client from the start" (#451 §7.4, Internal interfaces provided — public), and names this task by number as that second client: "`.dig` (#612) is its designed second client, so the hardening work is written and reviewed once" (#451 §7.5, Internal interfaces provided — private; the same sentence recurs in #451 §12, Related Work). This task therefore does not design or review its own separate XML-hardening configuration; it consumes #451's.

records.title: [BUG] Claude Desktop: hardcoded 60s initialize timeout drops stdio MCP servers whose package-runner cold start exceeds it
records.body:
## Summary

Claude Desktop cancels the MCP `initialize` request after **exactly 60 seconds** and there is no way to raise that limit. For `stdio` servers launched through a package runner (`uvx`, `npx`, `pipx run`), the download+install of dependencies happens *inside* that 60s window, before the server process exists. Any dependency refresh that pushes cold start past 60s therefore drops the server permanently for that session.

This is not a hypothetical: a routine upstream release of a transitive dependency (`botocore`, which ships a new version **every business day**) is enough to take a working configuration to a fully broken one overnight, with no change on the user's side.

## Environment

- Claude Desktop **1.25927.0** (macOS 26.5.2, arm64)
- 3 × `stdio` MCP servers, identical launcher: `uvx --with 'mcp[cli]<2' opensearch-mcp-server-py`
- `uv` 0.8.3

## What happens

From `~/Library/Logs/Claude/mcp-server-<name>.log`, identical in all three servers:

```
10:42:46.158Z [info] Initializing server...
10:42:46.170Z [info] Server started and connected successfully
10:42:46.194Z [info] Message from client: method="initialize" id=0
              Downloading botocore (14.8MiB)
10:43:46.215Z [info] Message from client: method="notifications/cancelled"   <-- +60.000s
10:43:46.216Z [info] Client transport closed
10:43:48.229Z [info] Server transport closed
```

The cancellation lands 60.000s after `initialize` — a fixed deadline, not a network failure. The servers' tools are then absent from the session entirely.

Measured by hand, same command, same env:

| Condition | Time to `initialize` response |
|---|---|
| Cold (dependency resolution + download of 68 packages) | **110 s** |
| Warm (uv cache populated) | 7–26 s |

Warm start succeeds and the servers work perfectly. So the only thing standing between "works" and "silently gone" is whether an upstream package published a release since the last launch.

## Root cause chain

1. The MCP server package declares `boto3>=1.39.0` — an open upper bound.
2. `botocore` releases daily (24 releases in July 2026 alone).
3. `uvx` resolves to the newest match on each launch; a new `botocore` invalidates the cached environment and triggers a fresh 14.8 MB download (occasionally `numpy`/`scipy`/`scikit-learn` too, ~50 MB total, 68 packages).
4. Cold install takes ~110 s > 60 s deadline → `notifications/cancelled`.
5. All three servers race for the same uplink simultaneously, making each slower.

Evidence that step 3 happens routinely: the local `uv` cache holds **42 separate environments spanning 15 botocore versions** (1.43.46 … 1.43.64), and has grown to **11 GB**. `botocore` 1.43.64 was published at 20:12 the previous day; the failure above is from the next morning's first launch.

## Why `notifications/progress` cannot solve this

The usual answer to a slow `initialize` is for the server to emit progress notifications and let the client extend its deadline. **That is structurally impossible here.** During the download there is no server process yet — `uvx` is still assembling the environment that will contain the server. Nothing exists that could send a notification. A client-side configurable deadline is the only thing that can help.

## Why existing issues don't cover this

- #43791, #22542, #16837, #3033, #20335 — all about **tool call / request** timeouts, not the `initialize` handshake.
- #60224 — closest, but Claude Code **CLI** on Windows and a session-init *probe*; closed as not planned.
- #26666 — lazy init to unblock the prompt; closed as duplicate. Related but orthogonal: lazy init alone would still cancel this handshake.
- #64671 — Windows `UtilityProcess` **spawn** timeout (5 s, OS-level), a different stage.

What is specific here: **Claude Desktop**, the **`initialize`** stage, and a server that has **not started yet** because its package manager is still installing it.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Configure a `stdio` MCP server launched via `uvx` with a package whose dependency tree is large and unpinned (any package depending on `boto3` works).
2. Run `uv cache clean` to simulate the state after an upstream dependency release.
3. Start Claude Desktop.
4. Observe `Downloading …` in the server log, then `notifications/cancelled` at exactly +60 s, and the server's tools missing from the session.

## Expected behaviour

Any one of these would resolve it:

1. **A configurable initialization timeout** — honour a `timeout` (or `initTimeout`) field per server in `claude_desktop_config.json`, or an `MCP_TIMEOUT` env var, for the `initialize` phase.
2. **Treat stderr activity as liveness** — the child process is demonstrably alive and writing `Downloading botocore (14.8MiB)` to stderr throughout. Resetting the deadline on output would fix the common package-runner case with no config.
3. **Retry / late attach** — if a server completes `initialize` after cancellation, register its tools rather than discarding them. The install finishes ~50 s later and the server sits there fully functional but unreachable.
4. At minimum, **surface the cause in the UI**. The server currently shows as failed with no hint that a download was cut short; a user reasonably concludes their backend is down and investigates in the wrong place.

## Current workaround

Pin the package version so resolution stops picking up new transitive releases, and pre-warm the cache manually before starting the app. Both require knowing about the 60 s deadline in the first place, which is only discoverable by reading the logs closely enough to notice the timestamps are exactly 60.000 s apart.

records.title: impact_analysis traverses relationships undirected, surfacing elements unrelated to the queried one via a shared type
records.body:
`impact_analysis` in `sysml_copilot/query.py` runs:

```cypher
MATCH path = (start:Element {id: $id})
             -[:CONNECTS_TO|TYPED_BY|SATISFIES*1..3]-(other:Element)
```

Note there's no `->`/`<-` on the relationship pattern — it matches `TYPED_BY` (and the other types) in *either* direction. For `CONNECTS_TO`/`SATISFIES` that's probably intended (impact is symmetric between two connected/satisfying parts). But `TYPED_BY` is not symmetric: it points from a usage to its type (`usage -[TYPED_BY]-> type`).

Concretely, using `data/sample.sysml`'s `FuelPort` (typed by `Engine.fuelIn`, `FuelTank.fuelOut`, `FuelPump.fuelIn`, `FuelPump.fuelOut`): querying the impact of `Engine.fuelIn` walks `TYPED_BY` forward to `FuelPort` (hop 1, reasonable — the port's type is affected... or rather, changing the port usage doesn't really affect the type, but that's a separate discussion), then *backward* from `FuelPort` to every other port usage typed by it — `FuelTank.fuelOut`, `FuelPump.fuelIn`, `FuelPump.fuelOut` — at hop 2, none of which have any real relationship to `Engine.fuelIn` beyond coincidentally sharing a type. On a real model where many usages share a common library type, this means impact analysis on almost any typed usage balloons to include every unrelated sibling usage of that type, which is a similar false-positive-flooding problem to the one `CONTAINS` exclusion (see README/CLAUDE.md `IMPACT_RELATIONSHIP_TYPES` note) was designed to avoid — but via `TYPED_BY` instead of `CONTAINS`.

Suggested fix: make the traversal direction-aware per relationship type instead of blanket-undirected — e.g. `TYPED_BY` should probably only traverse `usage -> type` (forward), not backward into sibling usages, while `CONNECTS_TO`/`SATISFIES` can stay undirected since those really are symmetric relationships between two specific elements. Would need a concrete pass/fail check on `data/sample.sysml` (e.g. impact of `Engine.fuelIn` should not include `FuelTank.fuelOut`/`FuelPump.fuelIn`/`FuelPump.fuelOut`) before/after the change.

Noticed while scanning `query.py` for gaps not yet covered by an existing issue (distinct from #6, which is about `CONTAINS` exclusion missing the queried element's own subtree — this is about `TYPED_BY` direction causing over-inclusion, not under-inclusion).

records.title: Pipeline visibility depends on the main checkout's branch, and nothing checks it
records.body:
Installing a plugin on a feature branch does not reach dispatched agents until it merges, which makes any ticket that both adds a plugin *and* depends on it unworkable.

## Observed root cause: the main checkout was on a branch without the harness

Diagnosed on the pilot repository. The cockpit prompted for permission to read a worktree's `port.config.json`, and the reason turned out to be upstream of worktrees entirely:

| Ref | Harness files present |
| --- | --- |
| main checkout, on branch `12-dark-light-mode` | **none** |
| `origin/dev` | `.claude/port.config.json`, `.claude/settings.json` |
| `origin/main` | none |

The install merged to the integration branch, but the operator's checkout was sitting on an **older feature branch that predates it**. So on disk there was no `.claude/settings.json` — **no permission rules at all** — and no config. Every read and every command falls back to prompting, and the pipeline's whole safety model (broad allow, authoritative deny, `dontAsk` auto-denying) is simply absent.

Nothing detected this. The cockpit started, ticked, dispatched, and only surfaced as a confusing permission prompt about a path inside a worktree.

**This is the same root variable as the plugin lag below: what the pipeline can see is a function of the branch the main checkout happens to be on, and nothing checks it.**

### Preflight the cockpit

`/port:pipeline` should refuse to start, with a specific message, when:

- `.claude/port.config.json` is absent on disk — it is not port-managed *on this branch*, even if the repository is managed on another. Say which branch is checked out and offer the one carrying the config.
- `.claude/settings.json` is absent, or carries no `permissions.allow`. Without it, stage agents cannot function: under `dontAsk` everything not allowlisted is denied, so an agent would fail every command for no visible reason.

Both are cheap file reads and both currently fail silently in ways that look like unrelated bugs. A cockpit that starts in this state is worse than one that refuses.

## Why it happens

Project-scoped installs write `enabledPlugins` and `extraKnownMarketplaces` into the repository's **committed** `.claude/settings.json`. That was the right call — it is what makes a repository self-describing and what carries a plugin into worktrees at all. The cost is that the declaration is branch state.

This is the same shape as a hazard already documented in `PIPELINE.md`:

> A worktree is a checkout of `<integration>`, so it carries the *committed* settings — **permission changes take effect for dispatched agents only after they merge.**

Per-repository plugin installs put plugins in that same category, and nothing says so.

## First, establish where the lag actually is — the fix depends on it

Two candidate mechanisms, and they call for different answers. **Verify before designing anything.**

1. **Plugin loading is session-level.** The cockpit session resolves plugins once at startup, from the main checkout — so what agents can use is whatever the main checkout's branch had *when the cockpit started*. A dispatched agent's worktree settings are then irrelevant to plugin availability, and merging is not sufficient either: the main checkout must be updated and the session reloaded.
2. **Plugin loading follows the working directory.** A subagent in a worktree resolves that worktree's `.claude/settings.json` — in which case merging to the integration branch genuinely is what unblocks it, since worktrees are cut from there.

Present belief is **(1)**, because a subagent runs inside the parent session's process rather than as a new session, and plugin resolution happens at session start. But the CLI clearly does resolve project settings from the current directory, so (2) is not absurd. **This has not been tested and the ticket should not proceed on the guess.**

## Mitigations worth considering, once that is known

- **Treat a plugin addition as its own prerequisite ticket.** The pipeline already models this — `blockedBy`, which the cockpit checks and warns about at opt-in. A ticket that adds a plugin merges first; tickets that rely on it declare it as a blocker. This needs no new machinery and is probably the main answer.
- **Warn when installing off the integration branch.** `/port:analyze` and `/port:init` should notice they are on a feature branch and say plainly that the install will not reach dispatched agents until it merges. Right now they report success with no such caveat, which is how this surprises someone.
- **Make the cockpit detect staleness.** On a tick it could compare the `enabledPlugins` it is running against what `origin/<integration>` now carries, and report a drift — "a plugin was added on the integration branch; pull and reload to pick it up". Cheap if mechanism (1) holds, and it turns an invisible lag into a reported one.
- **Document the ordering explicitly** in `PIPELINE.md`, beside the existing permissions hazard, so the two live together rather than one being a known trap and the other a surprise.

Deliberately **not** proposed: installing to `.claude/settings.local.json` for faster local effect. It is gitignored, so it never reaches a worktree — it would appear to fix the problem for the operator's own session while leaving agents exactly as blocked, which is worse than the current honest failure.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Determined and recorded whether plugin availability for dispatched agents follows the cockpit session or the worktree
- [ ] `PIPELINE.md` documents the plugin lag beside the existing permissions lag, with the actual required sequence
- [ ] `/port:analyze` and `/port:init` warn when installing a plugin from a non-integration branch
- [ ] The recommended workflow — plugin addition as a prerequisite ticket — is stated where an operator will meet it
- [ ] If mechanism (1) holds, the cockpit reports plugin drift against the integration branch rather than leaving it silent
